readerTitle: The best salesperson you know might be your plumber
caseNote: 가상 사례 (온수기 수리 기사, 회사 안의 재무운영팀) + 실제 저작 (Daniel Pink, To Sell Is Human)
insight: 판매는 상대를 설득해 사게 만드는 일이 아니라, 상대가 자기 문제에 대해 좋은 결정을 내리도록 돕는 일이다. 그래서 때로는 '지금은 사지 마세요'가 가장 좋은 판매가 된다.
misconception: 영업은 말 잘하는 사람이 상대를 밀어붙여 사게 만드는 일이고, 영업 직함이 없는 사람과는 상관없다.

sources.text: Pink, D. H. (2012). To Sell Is Human: The Surprising Truth About Moving Others. Riverhead Books.
온수기 수리, 재무운영팀 사례와 모든 금액은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Pink(2012)의 '비영업적 판매(non-sales selling)' 개념 설명을 원문으로 확인하세요. 책에 나오는 업무 시간 비율 수치는 확인 전이라 카드에 넣지 않았고, '상당한 시간'으로만 표현했습니다.
온수기 사례 금액($150 부품, $1,800 교체)은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 시세를 주장하지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.

cards.title: The best salesperson you know might be your plumber
body: Your water heater stops working. You expect a technician to quote a new one for $1,800.
Instead she replaces a $150 part and says, "This tank has a few good years left. When it goes, here's what to look for."
She sold you less today. You'll probably call her first for everything that breaks from now on.

image.label: A technician kneeling by a water heater, explaining to a homeowner
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 지하실에서 수리 기사가 온수기 옆에 무릎을 꿇고 작은 부품을 손바닥에 올려 집주인에게 보여줌. 집주인은 안도하는 표정. 실제 브랜드 로고나 제품명은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The customer asked for a replacement quote.
body: You run a small plumbing business. A homeowner calls and asks for a quote on a new water heater. You inspect it. It's twelve years old, but a $150 repair would likely fix today's problem.
A new unit would earn you far more. What do you do?

options.text: Quote the replacement. That's what they asked for
options.feedback: You win a bigger job today. If they later learn a cheap repair would have worked, you lose their trust and every job after it.

options.text: Do the repair and don't mention the tank's age
options.feedback: Honest and cheap for them, but they're left unprepared. When the tank fails, they may call whoever answers first.

options.text: Lay out both options, the costs and what to expect, then let them choose
options.feedback: You may earn less today. You earn the role of the person they trust with the decision, which is worth more over time.

cards.title: The small job became the big one.
body: The homeowner chose the repair. Two years later the tank failed for good. They didn't search online or compare three quotes. They called the same plumber and booked the $1,800 replacement.
Along the way, they told two neighbors about the plumber who "didn't try to upsell me." The repair looked like a lost sale. It was the start of a relationship.

cards.title: Selling is helping
body: **Selling is helping** someone with a problem make a good decision about whether, and how, to solve it.
The goal isn't to get a yes. It's to get the *right* answer for them, even when that answer is "not now" or "not from me."
A simple test: **would you give the same advice if you earned nothing from it?** If yes, you're helping. If no, you're pushing.

image.label: Two paths: pushing toward a yes versus guiding toward the right choice
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Pushing": 판매자가 고객 등을 떠미는 화살표, 목표는 "Yes". 오른쪽 "Helping": 판매자와 고객이 나란히 지도를 보며 갈림길 "Buy / Wait / Look elsewhere"를 고름.

cards.softwareNote: Telling a prospect that a cheaper plan covers their needs, or that another tool fits better, loses a little revenue today. It also means fewer refunds and cancellations, and customers who trust your next recommendation.

cards.title: You sell even without the job title.
body: In *To Sell Is Human* (2012), Daniel Pink argued that most people spend a large part of their work persuading others: pitching an idea to a boss, asking a team to change a process, getting a colleague to give up their time.
He called it "non-sales selling." The same rule applies. People say yes more readily, and stay committed, when they believe you're trying to solve their problem rather than yours.

image.label: Office scenes: a manager pitching a budget, a lead presenting a new process
image.brief: 사무실 장면 세 컷. 예산안을 설명하는 팀장, 새 업무 절차를 소개하는 담당자, 동료에게 협조를 부탁하는 직원. 각 컷 위에 작은 말풍선 "How does this help you?".

cards.title: Helping is not the same as being shy.
body: If your offer really fits someone's problem, staying vague or quiet isn't kindness. It leaves them stuck with the problem. Helping includes clearly saying, "I think this is right for you, and here's why."
And helping doesn't mean discounting or giving work away. A fair price for a real solution is part of the help.
If you rarely believe your offer fits, the issue isn't your sales style. It's the offer.

cards.title: Now you're selling inside the company.
body: You lead a finance operations team at a mid-sized company. You've built a new expense approval process. The sales department is resisting it and complaining that it adds steps.
How do you get them on board?

options.text: Ask the CFO to make the new process mandatory
options.feedback: You get compliance fast, but people work around rules they resent. The resistance just goes quiet.

options.text: Send a clear memo listing the new process's features
options.feedback: Clarity helps, but features describe your problem, not theirs. It doesn't show sales managers what's in it for them.

options.text: Sit with two sales managers, see what slows them down, show where the process saves them time and admit where it doesn't
options.feedback: It takes longer, but they see you solving their problem. Honesty about the costs makes your claims about the benefits believable.

cards.title: Help people decide well, and the sales follow.
body: Pushing wins one deal. Helping wins the next call, the referral and the benefit of the doubt.
**Try it today:** think of your next pitch, to a customer or a colleague. Ask yourself: would I give this same advice if I earned nothing from it? If not, change the advice.
